hooks.text: Three astronauts were suffocating inside a dying moon lander.
Could you build a life-saving machine with duct tape?
The Apollo 13 crew didn't survive because of high-tech gear.

title: Saving Apollo 13 With Duct Tape
description: How NASA engineers used literal trash to save three astronauts stranded in deep space after a catastrophic oxygen tank explosion.

beats.text: Three astronauts were suffocating inside a dying moon lander.
beats.visual: photograph of the Apollo 13 Lunar Module Aquarius in space, 1970

beats.text: It was like their spacecraft's lungs were slowly clogging up.
beats.visual: interior view of the crowded Apollo 13 Lunar Module cabin, 1970

beats.text: Poison gas spiked because Jim Lovell's crew crowded a two-man ship.
beats.visual: portrait of the Apollo 13 crew Jim Lovell Fred Haise and Jack Swigert, 1970
queries: Jim Lovell Fred Haise Jack Swigert

beats.text: The Command Module had square filters, but the Lander's holes were round.
beats.visual: NASA photograph of the square lithium hydroxide canisters, 1970

beats.text: They were stranded 200,000 miles from Earth with zero spare parts.
beats.visual: NASA view of Earth from the distance of the Moon, 1970

beats.text: Mission Control engineers built a fix using manuals and duct tape.
beats.visual: photograph of NASA engineers at Mission Control in Houston, 1970

beats.text: This 'mailbox' made of manuals and plastic saved their lives.
beats.visual: NASA photograph of the improvised mailbox air filter, 1970

beats.text: It's the only reason those three astronauts didn't end up suffocating.
beats.visual: photograph of the Apollo 13 command module splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, 1970
